Ever wonder if you should spin up a Databricks Lakebase instance or go with Snowflake Postgres for your workloads?

I’ve been comparing the two over the past few weeks.

Lakebase feels like a natural extension of the Databricks lakehouse.
It lets you run PostgreSQL queries directly on Delta tables.

Snowflake Postgres, on the other hand, offers a fully managed PostgreSQL engine that integrates with Snowflake’s cloud data platform.
In my tests the latency was lower on Lakebase for simple read‑heavy queries because the data never leaves the lake.
But Snowflake gave me better isolation and easier scaling for mixed OLTP/OLAP workloads.

Here’s what I took away:
- Choose Lakebase if your team lives in the Databricks ecosystem and you need fast access to Delta Lake data.
- Pick Snowflake Postgres when you want a dedicated PostgreSQL service with built‑in security and autoscaling.
- Consider cost and operational overhead – Lakebase can be cheaper for pure read workloads, Snowflake adds value for complex transaction patterns.

What’s your experience with managed PostgreSQL services and how do you decide which one fits your project?

concept_posts.post_content:
Ever wonder why your Spark jobs sometimes feel stuck on a single VM?

Running Spark on Kubernetes lets you treat each executor as a pod that the cluster can schedule dynamically.

Think of it like handing out tasks to a fleet of containers that can scale up or down based on demand.

When I first moved a batch pipeline to K8s,
I defined a SparkApplication CRD,
set the driver and executor images,
and let the scheduler handle the rest.

The result was smoother scaling and better resource isolation.

Key takeaways:
- Define resource requests and limits for driver and executors to avoid noisy neighbor issues.
- Use a stable Spark Docker image that matches your cluster’s Scala and Hadoop versions.
- Enable dynamic allocation so pods are added only when needed.

Common mistake: forgetting to set the proper service account,
which leads to permission errors when Spark tries to pull images or write to storage.

Have you tried Spark on Kubernetes yet?

concept_posts.post_content:
Ever found yourself scrambling because a teammate couldn't find the right customer table?
I’ve been there too.
In my last project we set up a simple data governance framework that kept everything discoverable and trustworthy.
Think of it like a library catalog for your data lake.
Every dataset gets a clear owner,
a documented purpose,
and a version tag.
When someone needed the latest sales figures they could just look up the catalog entry and know who to ask.
Here are a few habits that made a difference:

- Assign data owners early and keep their contact info in the catalog.
- Enforce schema contracts and automated quality checks at ingestion.
- Review access permissions quarterly to match business needs.
A common mistake is treating governance as a one‑time checklist instead of an ongoing habit.
If you skip the regular reviews,
stale definitions creep in and downstream pipelines break.
What’s one governance step you wish you’d started earlier?
#DataGovernance #DataEngineering #BestPractices #DataQuality
